Preface
This is a Quarto book.
The Preface, Introduction, Summary, and References page are automatically generated defaults for a Quarto book template, and I’ve left them to further demonstrate the structure.
The other two pages I wrote myself to demo some features and detail my experience installing a local LLM on Morpheus.
To see the actual book files, I have put them in a GitHub repository here

title: Handwritten Code: Translation and Execution
text:
I have detailed some of the handwriting translation techniques already

So I’ll start by explaining the execution environment that I build for the C++ code


Podman container setup
Podman is a rootless container alternative to Docker, and has nearly one-to-one support for Docker images.
For my image, I landed on an Alpine-based build for its small size, I install the g++ compiler and coreutils inside it for its timeout utility.
I also point to an entrypoint script - run.sh - that dictates how the C++ file is compiled and where stdout and stdin are directed.


Podman Run Options
podman run --rm \
--network none \
--read-only \
--read-only-tmpfs=false \
--tmpfs /tmp:size=50m \
--memory 256m \
--memory-swap 256m \
--cpus 0.5 \
--pids-limit 64 \
--timeout 60 \
--cap-drop ALL \
--user sandbox \
--security-opt no-new-privileges \
-v ./hello.cpp:/sandbox/source.cpp:ro \
sandbox:cpp
The command is very large, so I’ll break it down flag by flag

--rm: deletes the container after it is done running

--network none: disables all network functionality

--read-only: makes the file system read-only

--read-only-tmpfs=false: makes the temporary file system not read-only

--tmpfs /tmp:size=50m: mounts the temporary file system with a 50 mb size restriction

--memory 256m: restricts RAM usage to 256 mb

--memory-swap 256m: sets the swap to the same as the restriction

This effectively disables memory swap.


--cpus 0.5: throttles the container to only use up to half a CPU

--timeout 60: makes the container close itself after 60 seconds

There are other timeout restriction limits on ollama, compilation, and execution, but having extra doesn’t hurt.


--cap-drop ALL: removes all Linux kernel capabilities and privileges

--user sandbox: assigns the sandbox user created during image generation

-v ./hello.cpp:/sandbox/source.cpp:ro:

./hello.cpp is the example for the C++ file that is to be executed
/sandbox/source.cpp copies and mounts the file with a consistent filename in the given location
ro makes it read only.


sandbox:cpp is the image name

There may be additional options that make it more secure, but this is what I decided to go with for now, and what I ran all my tests with.


Manual Container Testing
I wrote some tests that would require the podman container to stop them, and I will include more details of the results of the full pipeline using the handwritten versions later.
For now, I will say that I tested the memory limit, network connection, pid limit, read-only file system (outside of tmp), and compilation failure.
After some debugging of my run.sh script, it was handling everything properly as far as I could tell from my tests.


Container Controller
When doing the testing manually, I had very limited information and my control and sight over stdout and stderr was limited.
There also were several manual steps to execution, like making the cpp file readable.
To solve this, I made a controller that formatted the stdout and stderr, and handled the file readability

Frontend Demo - Try It Yourself
I stitched together some of these elements and made a basic Python HTTP runner to deliver the translated code to the container to be ran, so there could be a frontend for this demo.

It’s important to note that this is not capable of handling concurrent users.

Even just one user submitting a request while another user’s is loading will not work.


When the service is started there is a simple frontend that will allow the user to upload an image of handwritten code

see /home/teig/start.sh, as well as status.sh and stop.sh there








Submission Screen


Then, there will be an intermediate “approval” step that will allow the user to edit the translated code, and then they can submit it afterwards







Edit Screen


The submission screen will display the stdout, stderr, status, exit code, and the submitted code that was ran in the podman container.







Result Screen

title: The Full Pipeline
text:
Full App Migration
I have migrated the demo into a much more robust Flask app, and it now supports several more features.

Session

A user has a session that keeps track of all the submissions (the timestamp, image, code results, etc.)

Session History

This is where the user can view all the information tracked by the current session in a summary screen
Includes an easy-to-read PDF export

Sessions History (history of all sessions)

A history of the current and past sessions, so progress isn’t accidentally lost

New Session

A user can start a new session anytime they choose
Once a session is ended, it is considered “archived” and cannot be changed


User sessions are built using a UUID system, so there is no login/logout or user state. The user’s session UUIDs are stored for 30 days in their cookies locally, and the site generates based upon that, using the information stored in the DB (and the images stored on the disk)

title: The Full Pipeline
text:
Full Pipeline load testing
I made a load_test.py script that allows for testing the full pipeline with concurrent requests.
I ran 5 consecutive load tests, each with 10 users and a different image each to go through the whole process each time.
Below are two different figures that I made based on the results of those tests.
The first shows the increasing wait time for each user, and the second shows the variance accounting for the increasing queue time.


Code
library(ggplot2)

times <- c(16.27, 18.28, 20.65, 22.92, 25.32, 27.47, 29.69, 32.43, 35.17, 37.53,
           17.85, 19.52, 21.31, 22.99, 24.80, 26.73, 28.46, 30.29, 32.15, 34.04,
           12.61, 14.14, 15.71, 17.51, 19.11, 20.73, 22.25, 24.02, 25.47, 27.35,
            9.62, 12.79, 16.02, 19.05, 22.72, 25.45, 28.85, 31.67, 35.50, 38.88,
            4.89,  6.65,  8.44, 10.20, 12.00, 13.78, 15.49, 17.29, 19.03, 20.86)

df <- data.frame(
  time = times,
  run = factor(rep(1:5, each = 10)),
  user_position = rep(1:10, times = 5)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = user_position, y = time, color = run)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(title = "Pipeline Completion Steadily Increases",
       x = "User position (order of finish)",
       y = "Elapsed time since test start (seconds)",
       color = "Run") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 1: Load test completion time by user order, across 5 test runs






Completion time increases steadily with each additional consecutive user in every run

This is consistent with a single-threaded bottleneck (the local LLM OCR process) queueing requests.

Run 5 starts fastest and stays lowest throughout, while Runs 1–4 cluster closer together

This matches my manual use of the LLM for OCR, occasionally it gets hung up or processes very quickly.
This variance has occured with the same image being translated over and over, so I don’t believe it likely that it differs entirely based on input.




Code
library(dplyr)

deltas <- df %>%
  group_by(run) %>%
  arrange(user_position) %>%
  mutate(delta = time - lag(time)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(delta))

ggplot(deltas, aes(x = user_position, y = delta, color = run)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
  labs(title = "OCR Bottleneck Adds ~2 Seconds per Additional User",
       x = "Nth consecutive user",
       y = "Added time vs. previous user (seconds)",
       color = "Run") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 2: Marginal time added per additional consecutive user, by run






Most runs add a fairly consistent ~1–2 seconds per additional consecutive user

gives a reasonable estimate of the actual per-request cost of the local LLM doing OCR under load.

Run 4 stands out with a higher (~3–3.8s) and less consistent cost, indicating the bottleneck isn’t always stable.

It may be worth investigating what factors contributed to this inconsistency, and if the LLM can be made to return more quickly and consistently under different parameters
